source.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Blake Bordelon; Alexander Atanasov; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.tranche_reason: The study derives scaling behavior in a random-feature model and compares predictions with experiments on vision and language tasks; its model and method differ from the original language-model scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites prior scaling-law results, which are not recorded as rows. Theoretical predictions are recorded where the paper derives a result about scaling. Values that cannot be read or assigned from the figures are not inferred.
record.test_reason: A theory paper: it derives scaling laws in a solvable random-feature model, then fits power laws on small vision and language experiments (Figure 1, Figure 7). The theoretical derivations are about a stylized linear model, not language models. Only the small Transformer/Wikitext fit and the CIFAR-5M image fits bear directly on versions (V1, V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors present a solvable linear random-feature model (DMFT) that reproduces several scaling phenomena. In it, time and model-size exponents differ, so compute-optimal training increases steps faster than parameters; finite-width and finite-data corrections accumulate over training; and ensembling is not compute-optimal. They add that feature learning yields better scaling than the linearized theory captures, and that this needs a theory of kernel evolution.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a dynamical mean-field theory for a projected random-feature model and compares some predictions with CIFAR-5M and Wikitext experiments; it does not reproduce the original large-language-model scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling changes with task and feature-spectrum exponents, data availability and reuse, and whether networks are linearized or feature-learning.

fits_no_version.finding: In a solvable random-feature model with power-law spectra, test loss scales as t^-(a-1)/b in time and N^-min(a-1,2b) in model size. The compute-optimal rule grows training time faster than model size, with exponents set by the task and spectral exponents a and b. Synthetic simulations confirm this (Figures 2 and 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical account: time and model-size exponents differ, implying an asymmetric compute-optimal split (time grows faster than N) that depends on data spectral structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature-learning CIFAR-5M networks show substantially different and better compute-optimal scaling than linearized networks and than the after-kernel prediction. The kernel keeps evolving during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel or random-feature theories capture lazy-regime scaling but underpredict feature-learning scaling exponents.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The analytical scaling results are for a stylized random-feature model; the realistic-network experiments are limited to CIFAR-5M and Wikitext. Several plotted results have no numerical values in the text, and the paper does not test small-run extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately stated results bearing on the listed versions were omitted.

untested.parts: Large language models, cross-entropy scaling over several orders of magnitude, and token or compute scaling for LMs. Only a small Wikitext Transformer with ~1.5 orders of width is tested.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
Not tested for LMs. The time-versus-model asymmetry is derived only in the random-feature model, and the CIFAR frontier gives no allocation exponents.
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Video, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. A power law in repeated data is not measured.
Not tested: no parameter-counting, schedule or fitting-method comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Fitted power-law form t^-0.16 + N^-0.76 for the Wikitext-100M Transformer (should be R6's value)

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical results are about a stylized MSE linear model, so they were removed from V1, V3 and V7 and recorded as fits_no_version. The experiments are small-scale (CIFAR-5M, Wikitext with 4096 maximum width). The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish the stated power laws for large language-model pretraining across several orders of magnitude. Its theory uses MSE in a random-feature model; the Wikitext experiments report qualitative width and data-reuse behavior, not a clearly stated fitted cross-entropy law.
No test of fitting laws on small runs and predicting much larger runs is reported.
The compute allocation is chiefly derived for the random-feature model with compute C = N t; it is not a direct fit of optimal parameter and token counts for large language models.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study covers CIFAR-5M and Wikitext, and discusses data reuse. It does not test video, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance prediction from pretraining loss is tested.
The study identifies dependence on task, spectral structure, data reuse, and feature learning, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions or fitting procedures.

rows.subject: random feature model
rows.size_stated: N is interpreted as model size; M, N, P large in the asymptotic theory
rows.operation_detail: Derives test-loss scaling with training time for power-law structured features
rows.note: This is a theoretical result for the paper's model, not a measured language-model pretraining exponent.
rows.check: Analytical result for a projected linear random-feature model trained on MSE, not held-out LM pretraining loss. It does not bear on V1. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: random feature model
rows.size_stated: N is interpreted as model size; P is dataset size
rows.operation_detail: Derives late-time test-loss scaling with model size and dataset size

conditions.value: t and the other resource tend to infinity

rows.measure: late-time test loss versus model size or dataset size
rows.value: L ∼ N⁻min{a−1,2b} and L ∼ P⁻min{a−1,2b}; for difficult tasks, both scale as the resource to the power −(a−1)
rows.note: The paper says the alternative exponents −2b occur for tasks satisfying a > 2b + 1, a condition it describes as rarely met in natural data.
rows.check: Theoretical model-size and data-size exponents of a random-feature model. This is not an LM measurement and not a comparison of fitting choices across published laws, so it bears on neither V1 nor V7. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: random feature model
rows.operation_detail: Derives the compute-optimal allocation between model size and training time

conditions.value: performance bottlenecked by training time or model size, not total data

rows.measure: optimal training time, model size, and test loss versus compute
rows.value: With m = min{a−1, 2b}, t ∼ Cᵃ⁻¹/(a−1+bm), N ∼ Cᵇᵐ/(a−1+bm), and L⋆(C) ∼ C⁻⁽ᵃ⁻¹⁾/(a−1+bm); when m = a−1, L⋆(C) ∼ C⁻⁽ᵃ⁻¹⁾/(1+b)
rows.note: The derived allocation makes training time scale faster than model size in the stated regime; as b → 1, the paper says they scale linearly together.
rows.check: Compute-optimal split derived for the random-feature model with C = N t. No LM parameter/token optimum is measured, so it does not bear on V3 or V7. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: residual CNN
rows.operation_detail: Measures test loss over training time and width on CIFAR-5M
rows.measure: test loss versus training time t and width N
rows.value: The figure reports a fit of the form L ∼ t⁻ᵅ + N⁻ᵝ; the plotted fit label is t⁻⁰·³⁸ + N⁻⁰·⁸¹
rows.note: The caption states that the fit describes the online test-loss behavior. The paper elsewhere identifies the CIFAR task as animate versus inanimate classification.
rows.check: Image classification with a residual CNN, so it bears on V5 (another modality), not V1 (LM loss). It also does not bear on V7: no fitting or setup choice is varied.

rows.subject: residual CNN
rows.operation_detail: Plots the compute-optimal test-loss frontier while varying model size and training time

conditions.value: proportional to model size times training steps

rows.value: The caption says the strategy scales up both model size and training time simultaneously
rows.note: The figure shows the compute-scaling result, but the caption does not give a numerical frontier exponent.
rows.check: Image task, so not V3 (LM params/tokens). The caption gives no frontier exponent and no allocation exponents, so the power-law form cannot be read from the text.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Plots train and test loss over tokens seen for different widths

conditions.value: train and test loss (cross-entropy, as described in Figure 1 caption)

rows.measure: train and test loss versus tokens seen and width
rows.value: The text states that model performance is monotonic in width N
rows.note: The stated width trend does not by itself establish that the loss follows a power law.
rows.check: Value is incomplete. The Figure 1(c) legend gives a fitted form t^-0.16 + N^-0.76 for the Wikitext-100M Transformer, and the intro says Figure 1 demonstrates scaling laws on language tasks. State should be observed for the power-law form, not cannot_determine. Widths span only 128–4096 (~1.5 orders) on a small dataset. V5 removed: this is text pretraining.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Plots train and test loss over tokens seen for different widths

conditions.value: train and test loss (cross-entropy, as described in Figure 1 caption)

rows.measure: train and test loss versus tokens seen and width
rows.value: The text states that larger width is not always better because wider models can overfit; Figure 1(d) caption describes overfitting and reversal of the wider-is-better phenomenon due to data reuse
rows.note: The paper reports a change in the width outcome under limited, repeated data.
rows.check: Repeated-data regime: wider models overfit and the wider-is-better trend reverses. V1 removed, because V1 excludes cases where data is the bottleneck. V7 removed, because no fitting or setup choice is compared. No power law in data or epochs is reported.

rows.subject: Wide ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Measures compute-optimal test-loss scaling for the linearized network using CIFAR-5M kernel spectra and task-power decay
rows.value: The predicted and plotted scaling is L⋆(C) ∼ C⁻⁰·⁰⁵; the text reports excellent agreement with the prediction
rows.note: This is an image-classification task and a linearized network, not language-model pretraining.
rows.check: Linearized (lazy) Wide ResNet on CIFAR-5M image classification, not LM pretraining, so V1 removed. Compute scaling C^-0.05 matches the theory's prediction.

rows.subject: feature-learning networks
rows.size_stated: Several widths and initialization seeds; Figure 7(c) shows N = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128
rows.operation_detail: Compares compute-optimal learning curves with those of linearized networks
rows.value: The paper reports substantially different compute-optimal scaling exponents and better loss curves for feature-learning networks; no numerical exponent is stated in the text
rows.note: The authors say the random-feature model captures linearized trends but does not capture the acceleration of scaling induced by feature learning.
rows.check: Compares the paper's linearized prediction with feature-learning networks. The text gives no exponent and does not say whether the curves follow a power law. This measures the adequacy of the theory, not a version.

rows.subject: Wide ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Measures the test loss over training time and compares it with a scaling prediction from the after-kernel
rows.value: The observed scaling is described as much better than that predicted from the after-kernel; the figure labels the prediction t⁻⁰·¹/¹·⁴
rows.note: The text states that the kernel continues evolving and that this improves the observed loss scaling relative to the prediction.
rows.check: Compares observed loss with an after-kernel-based prediction of the paper's own theory. The observed exponent is not stated. This bears on the theory, not a version.

relationships.condition: Small Transformer on Wikitext-100M, one pass before data repetition, widths 128–4096
relationships.reason: Loss falls monotonically with width, and the figure reports a fit of the form t^-0.16 + N^-0.76 (R6). The range is small.
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased monotonically with width and fit the form t^−0.16 + N^−0.76 over the measured range.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-5M image classification: online residual CNN, and linearized Wide ResNet compute frontier
relationships.reason: Test loss fits t^-0.38 + N^-0.81 (R4). The linearized compute-optimal loss follows C^-0.05 in agreement with the predicted scaling (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Online CNN test loss fit t^−0.38 + N^−0.81, while linearized compute-optimal loss followed C^−0.05 in agreement with predictions.

relationships.condition: Repeated data: Wikitext subsampled to 5M tokens
relationships.reason: With data reuse, wider models overfit and the wider-is-better trend reverses; no power law is reported in this regime (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Reusing the 5M-token Wikitext subset caused wider models to overfit and reversed the wider-is-better trend, without an established power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: The theory derives a compute-optimal allocation in which training time and model size both grow with compute, with exponents set by the task and feature spectrum (R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The compute-optimal exponents differ substantially between feature-learning and linearized networks, so the allocation is not captured by one model across these settings (R9).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: Feature learning gives substantially different compute scaling, and repeated-data Wikitext shows overfitting and a reversal of the width trend (R7, R9, R10).
